questions.q: State the chromosome number and DNA content in daughter cells immediately after mitosis if the parent cell was diploid (2n) with 2C DNA content at G1.
questions.a: Correct answer: Daughter cells are diploid (2n) with 2C DNA content. A wrong answer (e.g., 4C DNA or n chromosomes) reveals the student confuses mitosis with meiosis or misunderstands that DNA content halves only after cytokinesis completes, not during karyokinesis.

questions.q: Explain why a growing root tip cell must undergo mitosis after its cytoplasm expands during G1 and G2 phases.
questions.a: Correct answer: Cytoplasmic expansion increases the nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio beyond the optimal limit for nuclear control of metabolism; mitosis restores this ratio by dividing the nucleus and cytoplasm proportionally. A wrong answer focusing only on "growth" or "DNA replication" reveals the student misses the homeostatic principle of nucleo-cytoplasmic balance.

questions.q: A farmer notices that the sugarcane crop in his field regrows after harvesting the upper stalks. Identify the specific plant tissue and mitotic property enabling this regeneration.
questions.a: Correct answer: Intercalary meristem at the nodes; mitosis in these retained meristematic cells allows continuous longitudinal growth. A wrong answer naming apical meristem or cambium reveals confusion between primary growth (apical), secondary growth (lateral), and regrowth from nodes (intercalary).

questions.q: Trace the correct sequence of reasoning that contrasts mitosis in human skin with mitosis in a honeybee drone.
questions.a: The contrast runs: (1) Human skin cells arise from diploid somatic divisions (2) The drone develops from an unfertilised haploid egg (3) Mitosis in the drone's tissues is therefore haploid acting on haploid (4) Mitosis itself preserves whatever ploidy the dividing cell carries, diploid or haploid. A wrong answer that insists mitosis only occurs in diploid cells shows the student has missed that mitosis is equational, conserving the starting chromosome number in both cases.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Mitosis alone is sufficient for the long-term survival of a multicellular species." Justify your answer.
questions.a: Correct answer: False. Mitosis enables growth and repair within an individual's lifetime, but without meiosis and sexual reproduction, there is no genetic variation for adaptation, no gamete formation, and no species continuity across generations. A wrong answer agreeing reveals confusion between individual maintenance and species survival.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using onion root tips to demonstrate that mitosis is restricted to specific regions of a plant.
questions.a: Expected answer: Stain root tips with acetocarmine, squash, and observe under microscope. Count mitotic indices in 1 mm zones from tip upward. High index in apical 2-3 mm (meristem), near zero in mature zones. Poor answer: only staining without zonal comparison, revealing failure to link mitosis to spatial localization.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Mitosis is an equational cell division process in which a single diploid parent cell divides to produce two ______ identical diploid daughter cells, maintaining the chromosome number (2n) and DNA content (2C) across generations of somatic cells.
Fill in the blank: Observe a mango tree in your courtyard: it grows taller every year, heals bark wounds within weeks, and ______ new leaves each spring.
What is Mitosis? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Mitosis is an equational cell division process in which a single diploid parent cell divides to produce two genetically identical diploid daughter cells, maintaining the chromosome number (2n) and DNA content (2C) across generations of somatic cells.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Mitosis?
questions.a: Students believe mitosis occurs in all living cells of an organism throughout life.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain four distinct biological roles of mitosis (growth, repair, nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio maintenance, and asexual reproduction) with specific examples from plants and animals, and can justify why mitosis is restricted to diploid cells in most higher organisms but occurs in haploid cells of certain lower plants and.
